summary: Deep technical session focused on Private VPC networking (PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS) and how runtime features (KV cache, batching, quantization) behave in a private deployment. Agreed to run a 1-hour benchmark using NexusHealth sample traffic to validate latency and throughput under realistic egress/NAT patterns; Redwood to share architecture diagram and security pack. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~53 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (NexusHealth Platform), Leah Ortiz (NexusHealth Security), Tobias Klein (NexusHealth ML Infra)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone thanks for joining today, title says Private VPC deep dive, we'll cover networking plus some runtime perf details — Maya and I will lead. Quick intros?
[00:12] Rajiv: Rajiv here, Platform lead, we're running k8s on AWS across two regions, want to understand how Redwood Private will sit in our VPC and implications for NAT and DNS.
[00:22] Leah: Leah, security, SOC2/ISO questions and key management — we need to know key rotation and audit logs.
[00:29] Tobias: Toby, ML infra, want to validate latency for our realtime features, and how KV cache / batching interacts with quantized models.
[00:38] Maya: Great. We'll start with an overview of the Private deployment networking patterns, then runtime specifics — KV cache, batching, quant. We'll also call out benchmarking plan.

[02:05] Maya: On networking we support three common patterns: (1) PrivateLink from your VPC to Redwood control plane for API calls, (2) fully private control plane + data plane inside your network for on-prem, and (3) VPC peering for dedicated connections. For most customers we recommend PrivateLink because it avoids internet egress.
[02:33] Rajiv: Quick Q: if we use PrivateLink, does inference traffic egress out via NAT to reach model shards in Redwood infra or is it entirely inside our subnet?
[02:42] Maya: Good question. With PrivateLink, the control plane traffic goes over endpoint, but data plane (model GPUs) in Private deployment are in your cluster — so inference stays in your VPC. For Redwood hosted variants, we use interface endpoints and there is egress to Redwood's subnets, which may traverse NAT. Important to map which model variants are self-hosted vs hosted.
[03:10] Tobias: So in our plan we're doing Private (customer-managed data plane) right? We want GPUs in our subnets.
[03:18] Samir: Correct, NexusHealth asked for the Private package. That means GPUs live in your account; Redwood control plane talks over PrivateLink for management, metrics, and logs.

[04:20] Leah: For compliance we need KMS integration and audit logs. Does the Private control plane push logs back to Redwood or can we keep them local?
[04:30] Maya: We offer both. You can forward audit logs to your SIEM via our agents, or keep them local; control plane will surface events but customers can opt to retain copies internally. KMS integration supported — we have HSM/KMS plug-ins.

[06:05] Maya: Switching to runtime: the KV cache is implemented node-local by default for latency. That means each GPU node keeps its own prefix/KV cache for faster prefix hits. There's an optional shared Redis-backed KV cache for high-hit-rate multi-node workloads but that trades latencies.
[06:34] Tobias: If we shard requests across N pods and have node-local KV, what's the cold-start penalty?
[06:42] Maya: Cold starts are higher for node-local because the cache needs to warm per node. We recommend warmup traffic or sticky routing to keep hot sessions on the same node. For workloads with many concurrent users and high prefix reuse, our shared KV option reduces miss amplification but adds ~3-12ms depending on network topology.
[07:10] Rajiv: Sticky session routing — does Redwood support session affinity at the service mesh level or do we need to handle that in our ingress?
[07:18] Maya: Redwood's runtime includes a routing layer that can do affinity by request hash. In Private we can deploy the router as a daemonset in your VPC to minimize cross-node hops. We also expose headers for client-side affinity if you want to control it.

[09:00] Samir: On batching: we use adaptive continuous batching with a max batch window. Default is 20ms micro-batching with a tail-latency focus. You can tune batch size and window; bigger windows increase throughput but increase p95/p99.
[09:23] Tobias: Our SLO is p95 < 150ms for 1k concurrent users. How does batching affect that?
[09:30] Maya: If you push the window to 50-100ms you'll likely hit higher throughput but risk p95 jumps. For p95-sensitive endpoints we recommend 10-25ms windows and preferring KV cache to reduce compute. We can also set per-route policies in the config.

[11:12] Rajiv: Quantization — we've been experimenting with int8 and 4-bit. What's Redwood's guidance for private deployments? Any tooling?
[11:22] Maya: We support quantized model variants and maintain quality profiles. For many LLMs int8 gives ~2-3x speedup with minor quality loss; 4-bit (nf4/4-bit) can be 3-6x depending on lib support. We provide eval harnesses so you can run your prompt set against variants; SEs can run AB tests during the pilot. Note: quantization sometimes changes tokenization edge cases — run your critical prompts.
[12:05] Tobias: Does quantization change KV cache format or compatibility across nodes?
[12:12] Maya: No, KV cache is model-architecture-aware; quantized vs fp16 models keep compatible KV semantics only if model architecture is same. If you run a quantized variant of the same checkpoint, caches are compatible; cross-architecture or different opt kernels are not.

[13:40] Leah: From networking standpoint, we need to understand NAT behavior. Our EKS nodes sit in private subnets with NAT gateways for egress. If the control plane tries to reach back, will responses be NATed?
[13:52] Maya: Control plane comms originate from your control plane agents to Redwood endpoints over the PrivateLink interface. For metric shipping to external services (e.g., Datadog) you'd route via NAT. For model pulls (initial artifact download), if you allow HTTPS to Redwood artifact bucket through PrivateLink or S3 endpoints, you can avoid NAT egress.

[15:30] Rajiv: DNS — we run split-horizon DNS. Will Redwood endpoints resolve correctly inside our VPC?
[15:38] Maya: We publish DNS names you can resolve via the interface endpoints. For split-horizon you can import our zone into your Resolver rules. Some customers use Route53 inbound/outbound resolver rules. We'll share a DNS checklist.

[17:00] Maya: A couple of gotchas: (1) If you use shared KV backed by Redis ensure low-latency network path between GPUs and Redis, ideally colocate in same AZ. (2) NAT gateways add consistent egress IPs but also add cost; consider using Egress-only or PrivateLink where possible. (3) Subnet sizing: GPU nodes can be denser — reserve /24 per k8s pool depending on scaling needs.

[19:22] Tobias: For benchmarking, what's Redwood's recommended telemetry? I want token-level latency, batch sizes, and KV hit rates in traces.
[19:30] Maya: We emit token-level metrics and batch histograms. We integrate with Jaeger/OTel and can send traces to your collector. For bench we suggest: load generator with realistic inter-arrival times, warmup for 5-10 minutes to populate KV, then a 1-hour run capturing p50/p95/p99, throughput, avg batch size, and KV hit ratio. We'll provide a harness.

[22:05] Rajiv: If we hit a model-quality regression after quantizing, is there a safe fallback?
[22:12] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports versioned model rollouts with automatic fallback to fp16 variant on quality regression. You can set thresholds tied to eval sets; the router will route to fallback model variant automatically.

[24:40] Samir: On networking plan: Redwood will provide an architecture diagram showing PrivateLink flow, necessary endpoint policies, and required IAM for S3/artifact access. We'll also include recommended subnet sizes and example security group rules.

[26:15] Leah: We need to see the audit log fields — timestamps, user IDs, request IDs. Also which fields are PII.
[26:24] Maya: We'll send the SOC2 pack and a sample audit schema. Most fields are request id, timestamp, model id, route, user-id (if passed), but you can redact PII before shipping.

[28:50] Tobias: Performance numbers — can you share ballpark latency for fp16 vs int8 on A100 and similar?
[28:58] Maya: Ballpark: for a 13B model on A100, fp16 generation token-latency ~8-12ms per token with batching and KV hits; int8 can drop to 4-7ms per token. Real end-to-end depends on batch waits and I/O. We'll share a performance matrix.

[31:10] Rajiv: For the shared KV option using Redis, is there support for TLS and auth?
[31:18] Maya: Yes, Redis connections support TLS and AUTH. We recommend running managed Redis in your VPC and limiting access via SGs.

[33:00] Samir: Let's talk routing fallbacks — if a node is overloaded, does the router spill to a less optimized variant?
[33:10] Maya: We support policy-based fallback: you can define fallback to a lower-cost model variant or different region; router will prefer latency SLOs then cost. Automatic fallback can be enabled for critical endpoints.

[35:45] Tobias: A specific edge case — what happens to KV cache during an autoscale down event? Do we warm new pods?
[35:55] Maya: When we scale down we lose node-local caches; we recommend graceful drain hooks that drain traffic and optionally snapshot warm prefixes to a shared cache store (if you enable that). Otherwise expect transient increased latency as caches warm. For scale-up we pre-warm by replaying recent traffic depending on policy.

[38:20] Rajiv: Ok on egress costs — if we can avoid NAT by using PrivateLink and S3 endpoints, that's preferable. Need example CloudFormation/terraform snippet.
[38:30] Samir: We'll include CF/Terraform snippets in the doc pack.

[40:05] Leah: On key management — can Redwood use our KMS for encrypting model artifacts, or do they need Redwood-managed keys?
[40:14] Maya: For Private we can integrate with customer KMS for artifact encryption and at-rest disk encryption; control plane metadata can be optionally encrypted with customer keys. We'll cover required IAM perms in the checklist.

[42:00] Samir: Quick recap of bench plan — Maya will coordinate a 1-hour run. Rajiv/Tobias will supply sample workload and model config. We will collect token-level metrics, batch histograms, and KV hit rates, and then review in follow-up.

[42:25] Rajiv: Timeline — we want a pilot in two weeks.
[42:30] Samir: We can aim for that pending benchmark results and your infra readiness.

[44:10] Maya: Shared artifacts — I'll drop a deck and a network checklist: https://redwood.example.com/docs/private-vpc-checklist (placeholder link), and the benchmark harness: https://redwood.example.com/bench/harness.

[46:00] Tobias: A few quick questions: how do you handle DNS caching when we use split-horizon? Any TTL recommendations?
[46:10] Maya: Use short TTLs (30-60s) on endpoint records during rollout, then increase. Also ensure your resolver forwards to the Route53 inbound resolver for the region. We'll provide sample resolver rules.

[48:45] Leah: Security follow-ups — pen test windows, contact for escalation, and what data is considered PII in logs.
[48:52] Samir: We'll include contact list and pen test policy.

[50:05] Rajiv: Wrap up — agreeable next steps?
[50:10] Samir: Confirmed next steps: share diagram + SOC2 pack, run benchmark, share pricing, schedule follow-up. Anything else?
[50:22] Leah: That's it from security.
[50:26] Tobias: Good.
[50:30] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with artifacts and the benchmark plan.
[50:36] Rajiv: Thanks all.

[51:00] (call end)
